case.title: A Mathematical Theory of Communication (C. E. Shannon, 1948), Section 6 Choice, Uncertainty and Entropy
case.excerpt: 6. Choice, Uncertainty and Entropy. Suppose we have a set of possible events whose probabilities of occurrence are p_1, p_2, ..., p_n. These probabilities are known but that is all we know concerning which event will occur. Can we find a measure of how much "choice" is involved in the selection of the event, or of how uncertain we are of the outcome? If there is such a measure, say H(p_1, p_2, ..., p_n), it is reasonable to require of it the following properties: (1) H should be continuous in the p_i. (2) If all the p_i are equal, p_i = 1/n, then H should be a monotonic increasing function of n: with equally likely events there is more choice, or uncertainty, when there are more possible events. (3) If a choice be broken down into two successive choices, the original H should be the weighted sum of the individual values of H. Theorem 2: The only H satisfying the three above assumptions is of the form H = -K sum_{i=1}^{n} p_i log p_i, where K is a positive constant (it merely amounts to a choice of a unit of measure). Quantities of the form H = -sum p_i log p_i play a central role in information theory as measures of information, choice and uncertainty, and will be recognized as the entropy of statistical mechanics. With logarithms to the base 2, the unit is the bit. Properties of H: (1) H = 0 if and only if all the p_i but one are zero, this one having the value unity; thus only when we are certain of the outcome does H vanish, otherwise H is positive. (2) For a given n, H is a maximum and equal to log n when all the p_i are equal (i.e., 1/n); this is also intuitively the most uncertain situation. For two possibilities with probabilities p and q = 1 - p, H = -(p log p + q log q), which is plotted as a function of p in Fig. 7.
case.focus: Explain discrete entropy (Section 6, H = -sum p_i log2 p_i) using a small probability distribution. Let the learner change the distribution and the number of outcomes. Show probabilities, individual contributions, and total entropy in bits. Compare a certain outcome with equally likely outcomes. Check that certainty gives zero bits and four equally likely outcomes give two bits; handle zero probabilities correctly.
case.audience: Engineering undergraduate who knows basic probability and logarithms but has not studied information theory.

plan.concept: Discrete entropy H = -sum p_i log2 p_i as a measure of choice/uncertainty, with the special cases H=0 for certainty and H=log2 n for equally likely outcomes.
plan.anchor: Section 6, Theorem 2 and Properties (1)-(2); Fig. 7 for the two-outcome case
plan.computation: Normalize the entered weights into probabilities p_i, compute each contribution -p_i log2 p_i (with 0 log 0 = 0), sum to H, and also report log2 n, the maximum, and the gap H_max - H.
plan.visual: Left: a bar chart of the probabilities p_i. Right: a stacked/individual bar chart of the contributions -p_i log2 p_i with a horizontal reference line at H and a dashed line at log2 n.
plan.controls: n (number of outcomes), a weight vector of length n, a preset select (certain / uniform / skewed), and a toggle to show the contribution bars.
plan.checks: Probabilities sum to 1; every p_i in [0,1]; H >= 0; H = 0 iff one p_i = 1; H <= log2 n with equality iff all p_i = 1/n; contributions sum to H.

spec.title: Entropy: How Much Choice Is in a Distribution?
spec.hook: Shannon asked how much "choice" or uncertainty a set of probabilities contains. Build a small distribution and watch the entropy in bits rise toward $\log_2 n$ as the outcomes become equally likely, and fall to zero when one outcome is certain.
spec.idea:
Suppose you are about to observe one of $n$ events, and you know only the probabilities $p_1,\dots,p_n$. Shannon asked for a number $H(p_1,\dots,p_n)$ measuring how much choice is involved. He required three things: $H$ is continuous in the $p_i$; when all outcomes are equally likely $H$ increases with $n$; and splitting a choice into two successive choices makes $H$ the weighted sum of the parts.

Theorem 2 says the only function satisfying these is $H = -K\sum_i p_i \log p_i$, with $K>0$ just fixing the unit. Taking base-2 logarithms makes the unit the **bit**.

Each term $-p_i\log_2 p_i$ is that outcome's own contribution. A very likely outcome contributes little (it is not surprising), and a very unlikely one also contributes little (it rarely happens) — the largest single contribution comes from an outcome with probability $1/e \approx 0.368$. The total $H$ is the sum of these contributions.

Two special cases anchor the intuition. If one outcome has probability 1, every term is zero, so $H=0$: certainty means no choice. If all $n$ outcomes are equally likely, $p_i = 1/n$ and $H = -\sum (1/n)\log_2(1/n) = \log_2 n$, the largest value possible for that $n$.
spec.why: Entropy is the currency of information theory: it sets the minimum average number of bits needed to describe the outcome of a random source, and it is the quantity that channel capacity and coding theorems are measured against. Getting comfortable with $H=-\sum p_i\log_2 p_i$ on a tiny distribution makes those later results readable.

equations.caption: Theorem 2: the unique measure of choice/uncertainty satisfying Shannon's three requirements; $K>0$ only chooses the unit.
The same formula with base-2 logarithms, so that $H$ is measured in bits.

equations.tex: H = 0 \iff p_i = 1 \text{ for exactly one } i
equations.caption: Property (1): entropy vanishes only when the outcome is certain.

equations.tex: H \le \log_2 n, \quad H = \log_2 n \iff p_i = 1/n \ \forall i
equations.caption: Property (2): for fixed $n$, entropy is maximized by the uniform distribution.
The two-outcome case plotted in Fig. 7; it peaks at $p=q=1/2$ with $H=1$ bit.

spec.visual_caption: Left panel: bars are the probabilities $p_i$ (blue), with a dashed line at $1/n$. Right panel: bars are the individual contributions $-p_i\log_2 p_i$ (one color per outcome), the solid horizontal line marks the total $H$, and the dashed line marks $\log_2 n$. The gap between the two lines is how far the distribution is from uniform. Bars of height zero mean that outcome contributes nothing.

explorations.title: Certainty gives zero bits
explorations.change: Look at the distribution with one weight equal to 1 and the rest 0, then drag the other weights up a little and back to 0.
explorations.observe: The $H$ value label reads 0.000 bits and every contribution bar has height 0; as soon as any other weight becomes positive, $H$ becomes positive.
explorations.why: Every term is $-p_i\log_2 p_i$ with $p_i$ either 0 or 1, and both give 0 (using $0\log 0 = 0$). Property (1) of the excerpt: only when we are certain of the outcome does $H$ vanish.

explorations.title: Four equally likely outcomes give two bits
explorations.change: Set $n$ to 4 and make all four weights equal. Then change $n$ to 2, 3, 5, 6 and watch the $H$ label.
explorations.observe: With $n=4$ equal weights the $H$ label reads 2.000 bits and the solid line sits exactly on the dashed $\log_2 n$ line. Changing $n$ moves the dashed line to $\log_2 n$ and $H$ follows it whenever the weights stay equal.
explorations.why: For equal probabilities $p_i = 1/n$, so $H = -\sum (1/n)\log_2(1/n) = \log_2 n$. With $n=4$ that is $\log_2 4 = 2$ bits; this is the maximum for that $n$, Property (2).

pitfall.title: Entropy is not the number of outcomes
pitfall.text: A distribution over 6 outcomes can have less entropy than one over 2 outcomes: set $n=6$ with weights $[1,0,0,0,0,0]$ and $H=0$, while $n=2$ with weights $[1,1]$ gives $H=1$ bit. Entropy depends on the whole distribution, not on $n$ alone; $n$ only sets the ceiling $\log_2 n$.

grounding.paper: A Mathematical Theory of Communication (C. E. Shannon, 1948)
grounding.section: Section 6, Choice, Uncertainty and Entropy; Theorem 2 and Properties (1)-(2); Fig. 7
from_source: Shannon considers a set of possible events with known probabilities $p_1,\dots,p_n$ and asks for a measure $H(p_1,\dots,p_n)$ of how much choice or uncertainty is involved.

He requires: (1) $H$ continuous in the $p_i$; (2) $H$ monotonic increasing in $n$ when all $p_i = 1/n$; (3) breaking a choice into two successive choices makes the original $H$ the weighted sum of the individual values.
Theorem 2: the only $H$ satisfying these is $H = -K\sum_{i=1}^n p_i \log p_i$ with $K>0$, where $K$ merely chooses the unit.
With logarithms to base 2 the unit is the bit.
Property (1): $H=0$ if and only if all $p_i$ but one are zero, that one being 1; only when certain of the outcome does $H$ vanish, otherwise $H$ is positive.
Property (2): for a given $n$, $H$ is maximum and equal to $\log n$ when all $p_i$ are equal to $1/n$.
For two possibilities with probabilities $p$ and $q=1-p$, $H = -(p\log p + q\log q)$, plotted against $p$ in Fig. 7.
our_additions: The interactive weight-vector normalization $p_i = w_i/\sum_j w_j$ is our device for letting the learner edit a distribution while keeping it valid.
The claim that the largest single contribution $-p_i\log_2 p_i$ occurs at $p_i = 1/e$ is our own calculus remark, not from the excerpt.
The preset names (equally likely, certain outcome, skewed) and the specific toy weights are ours.
The stacked-bar visual layout, the color coding, and the $H_{\max}-H$ gap readout are our presentation choices.
grounding.disclaimer: This page is a small interactive illustration of the entropy formula from Section 6. It does not reproduce any experiment, table or figure from Shannon's paper; all displayed numbers come from the current control settings.
